name: Awarua / Haast Visitor Centre
summary: Department of Conservation visitor centre, Haast

name: Moraine Lake
summary: A glacial lake below the Valley of the Ten Peaks, reached only by Parks Canada shuttle or licensed operator. No cell service, running water or other services at the lake.

name: Lake Louise
summary: Turquoise lake coloured by glacial rock flour, below Mount Victoria and its glacier, with the Chateau on its eastern shore. Shuttle from the Park and Ride, or paid lakeshore parking.

name: Peyto Lake
summary: A turquoise lake seen from a viewing platform near Bow Summit, a short walk from the Icefields Parkway 43 kilometres north of Lake Louise.

name: Bow Lake
summary: A large lake beside the Icefields Parkway about 37 kilometres north of Lake Louise, with a summer picnic area; Crowfoot Glacier viewpoint is just south.

name: Johnston Canyon
summary: A limestone gorge off the Bow Valley Parkway, walked on railed walkways and bridges past falls and pools. Trail and day-use area closed for construction until 11 December 2026.

name: Lake Minnewanka
summary: A reservoir north-east of the town of Banff, and the only water in the park where boats with motors, gas or electric, are allowed.

name: Cave and Basin National Historic Site
summary: The hot springs where the park began in 1885, sacred to many Indigenous nations, with an exhibit on the First World War internment camps.

name: Banff Upper Hot Springs
summary: A Parks Canada outdoor hot pool on Sulphur Mountain with views of Rundle and Cascade mountains, drawing bathers since 1886.

name: Banff Visitor Centre
summary: Parks Canada information and trail advice at 224 Banff Avenue in the town of Banff, and one of two places to get a random-camping permit in person.

name: Lake Louise Visitor Centre
summary: Parks Canada information in the village of Lake Louise, and the other place to get a random-camping or mountaineering bivouac permit in person.

name: Athabasca Glacier
summary: The Columbia Icefield's best-known glacier, beside the Icefields Parkway. The Toe of the Glacier and Forefield trails approach it; go onto the ice only with a guide or tour.

name: Maligne Lake
summary: A 22-kilometre glacial lake at the end of the Maligne Lake Road, with tour boats to Spirit Island and three backcountry canoe campgrounds. Gas motors are banned.

name: Athabasca Falls
summary: The Athabasca River drops 24 metres over hard quartzite into a short gorge, 30 kilometres south of Jasper, with viewing platforms and trails.

name: Sunwapta Falls
summary: A waterfall on the Sunwapta River, 54 kilometres south of Jasper just off the Icefields Parkway, with a picnic site.

name: Medicine Lake
summary: A lake on the Maligne Lake Road that drains through sinkholes in its bed; much of the Maligne River runs underground from here to Maligne Canyon.

name: Pyramid Lake
summary: A lake on the bench above town below Pyramid Mountain, with a beach and Pyramid Island day-use area. Electric motors only.

name: Miette Hot Springs
summary: The hottest springs in the Canadian Rockies, up the Fiddle valley: water leaves the mountain at 54 °C and is cooled to 40 °C for the pools. Closed in winter.

name: Valley of the Five Lakes
summary: A trail to five small lakes south of town off the Icefields Parkway, reopened in summer 2026 with a realigned section and new rest areas after the wildfire.

name: Jasper Park Information Centre
summary: Parks Canada's information centre on Connaught Drive in the town, built in 1913 and a national historic site; open all year.

name: Columbia Icefield Discovery and Information Centre
summary: Summer-only information centre by the Athabasca Glacier on the Icefields Parkway, 104 kilometres south of Jasper.

name: Takakkaw Falls
summary: Canada's second-highest waterfall, reached by a flat, paved 0.9-kilometre path at the end of Yoho Valley Road, 17 kilometres from Field. The road opens mid-June to mid-October.

name: Emerald Lake
summary: A green lake ringed by peaks, with a lodge and a 5.2-kilometre shoreline loop. The road from the Trans-Canada Highway is open all year.

name: Lake O'Hara
summary: An alpine lake ringed by high routes, reached by reserved bus, an 11-kilometre walk, or a stay at the lodge, hut or campground. Best hiking July to late September.

name: Spiral Tunnels Viewpoint
summary: Watch trains disappear into one tunnel and emerge from another at a different height; 25 to 30 pass daily, on no fixed schedule. Closed mid-October to mid-May.

name: Walcott Quarry
summary: The classic Burgess Shale fossil site, open only to Parks Canada guided hikes: 24 kilometres and 900 metres of climbing from Takakkaw Falls in about 11 hours.

name: Mount Stephen
summary: The peak above Field, with Burgess Shale trilobite beds reached on a steep guided hike of 8 kilometres and 800 metres of climbing from the visitor centre.

name: Wapta Falls
summary: The widest waterfall on the Kicking Horse River: a family walk of 2.2 kilometres each way, near the park's west boundary. Its road closes late October to late May.

name: Kicking Horse Pass National Historic Site
summary: The highest point on the Trans-Canada Highway, at the park's eastern edge, where the railway crossed the Great Divide and opened British Columbia to the rest of Canada by rail.

name: Yoho National Park Visitor Centre
summary: On the Trans-Canada Highway in Field, with park staff, a small Burgess Shale fossil exhibit and the Friends of Yoho shop. Open 1 May to 12 October in 2026.

name: Marble Canyon
summary: A narrow canyon followed by a 0.9-kilometre trail along its rim, with interpretive signs, bridges to look down from and Red Chairs at the end.

name: Paint Pots
summary: A gentle one-kilometre walk to three iron-rich mineral springs that stain the surrounding earth; the Ochre Creek area was long a source of pigment.

name: Stanley Glacier
summary: A 4.9-kilometre trail climbing 405 metres towards the glacier. Parks Canada's guided Burgess Shale fossil hikes start from this trailhead.

name: Floe Lake
summary: A lake below the limestone cliffs of the Rockwall, 10.8 kilometres and 1,120 metres of climbing from the highway: a popular day hike, with a backcountry campground.

name: Fireweed Loop, Vermilion Pass
summary: A 15-minute loop on the Continental Divide through forest regrowing since the Vermilion Pass wildfire of 1968.

name: Kootenay Valley Viewpoint
summary: A pull-out on Highway 93 South overlooking the Kootenay valley.

name: Olive Lake
summary: A small lake with a lakeshore boardwalk, 12 kilometres from Radium Hot Springs. Check the trail report for spring closures for bears.

name: Sinclair Canyon
summary: The narrow canyon at the park's south-west gate, widened by hand for the original road; a 2.8-kilometre trail follows its rim and drops into it.

name: Radium Hot Springs
summary: Parks Canada hot pools in Sinclair Canyon, 37 to 40°C and odourless, with a cool swimming pool, in the 1951 Aquacourt, a classified Federal Heritage Building.

name: Kootenay National Park Visitor Centre
summary: Shared with Tourism Radium at 7556 Main Street East in the village of Radium Hot Springs, with a Ktunaxa exhibit; Parks Canada staff from May to mid-October.

name: Rogers Pass
summary: The summit of the Selkirks crossing, a national historic site since 1971. A monument, the Abandoned Rails trail along the 1885 grade and the site of the 1910 avalanche.

name: Illecillewaet Glacier
summary: The 'Great Glacier' of the railway era, now about 1.5 kilometres further up its valley. The Great Glacier and Glacier Crest trails climb towards it from the Illecillewaet valley.

name: Mount Sir Donald
summary: The landmark peak above the Illecillewaet valley, named for the railway director who drove the last spike. A steep trail climbs to a climbers' bivouac below it.

name: Glacier House ruins
summary: Foundations of the railway's hotel below the Great Glacier, which offered meals, guided climbs and cave tours until it closed in 1925.

name: Loop Brook
summary: Giant stone pillars that carried the railway's loops across the valley, among the oldest surviving built structures in western Canada, on a 1.7-kilometre interpretive loop.

name: Hemlock Grove Boardwalk
summary: A 350-metre barrier-free boardwalk through towering cedar and hemlock rainforest, beside the highway west of Rogers Pass.

name: Balu Pass
summary: A steep 12.8-kilometre return hike through avalanche paths to alpine meadows. Grizzly country: groups of four adults required from mid-July to September, and no dogs.

name: Avalanche Crest
summary: One of the park's best scenic trails, into an alpine basin above the highway corridor; the treeless slopes below show where winter avalanches run.

name: Bear Creek Falls
summary: A short, steep trail down to a glacial waterfall, 9 kilometres east of the Rogers Pass Centre.

name: Summit Station
summary: The temporary visitor hub beside the Rogers Pass Centre, which is closed for rehabilitation: park information, passes, winter permits and washrooms.

name: Mount Revelstoke summit
summary: A 1-kilometre walk by trail or closed road from Balsam Lake, with views of the Monashee and Selkirk ranges and a network of short meadow trails.

name: Fire Lookout
summary: A lookout built in 1927 and staffed until 1988, now a Federal Heritage Building with a viewing platform, a short steep walk from the Upper Summit Shelter.

name: Heather Lake
summary: A small summit lake on a 400-metre loop, among at least three species of mountain heather in red, white and pale yellow.

name: Balsam Lake
summary: The end of the public road at kilometre 24 of the parkway, with summit parking, a picnic shelter and a 500-metre loop around the lake.

name: Eva Lake
summary: A 14.2-kilometre return hike across alpine meadows and boulder fields to a lake with a 1920s warden cabin and a backcountry campground. Snow-free mid-July to September.

name: Miller Lake
summary: A 27-metre-deep glacial bowl, 400 metres off the Eva Lake trail; a point jutting into the water makes a lunch stop.

name: Jade Lakes
summary: The upper and lower lakes beyond Jade Pass, the longest summit day hike at 18.8 kilometres return, with a backcountry campground.

name: Giant Cedars Boardwalk
summary: A 500-metre boardwalk through old-growth western red cedar, some trees over 500 years old, 30 kilometres east of Revelstoke on the Trans-Canada Highway.

name: Skunk Cabbage Boardwalk
summary: A 1.2-kilometre boardwalk through a wetland beside the Illecillewaet River, with three viewing platforms.

name: Nels Nelsen Historic Area
summary: The historic ski jump where world records were set between 1916 and 1933, at the foot of the parkway, with trails open all year.

name: Columbia Viewpoint
summary: Kilometre 12 of the parkway, looking over the Columbia valley to the Selkirk Mountains; dogs may go no further.

name: Snowforest Welcome Centre
summary: At Snowforest Campground, near the bottom of the parkway: park information, passes and backcountry permits, May to October.

name: Bear's Hump
summary: A 2.8-kilometre return trail to one of the park's best-known viewpoints, starting across the Entrance Road from the Prince of Wales Hotel access road.

name: Prince of Wales Hotel
summary: A chalet-style railway hotel with a timber-framed interior, opened by the Great Northern Railway in 1927 on a glacial kame above Upper Waterton Lake; a national historic site.

name: Cameron Falls
summary: A waterfall in Waterton townsite on the townsite loop path, beside the trailhead of the Alderson–Carthew route.

name: Red Rock Canyon
summary: A gorge of red and green argillite at the end of the 15-kilometre Red Rock Parkway, with a 0.7-kilometre loop trail. Open to cars May to late October.

name: Cameron Lake
summary: A cirque lake at the end of the Akamina Parkway, whose southern end reaches across the border into Montana, with a 3-kilometre return lakeshore trail.

name: Crypt Lake
summary: A 17.2-kilometre return day hike from a boat landing across Upper Waterton Lake, past waterfalls and through a tight tunnel onto a cliff ledge. Book the boat shuttle.

name: Bertha Lake
summary: A mountain lake 10.4 kilometres return from the townsite, passing Lower Bertha Falls; the trailhead lies in an avalanche path, so check the daily Bertha-Townsite advisory.

name: Upper Waterton Lake
summary: The lake in a glacier-carved valley that crosses the international border. The MV International, built in 1927, still carries boat tours on it.

name: Waterton Lakes Visitor Centre
summary: The new Parks Canada centre at 404 Cameron Falls Drive, open all year, with permits, backcountry bookings, trail and avalanche reports, and exhibits on Blackfoot culture.

name: Astotin Lake
summary: The park's centre for picnics, beach, campground and paddling, with many small islands. Canoes, kayaks and paddleboards can be rented; motorboats are not allowed.

name: Living Waters Boardwalk
summary: A 400-metre floating boardwalk loop out onto Astotin Lake, with exhibits; 15 to 30 minutes and ideal for small children.

name: Elk Island Pavilion
summary: An open-air shelter above the beach built by Depression-era relief workers in the 1930s, the oldest picnic shelter with a chimney in Canada's national parks.

name: Ukrainian Pioneer Home
summary: A reconstructed pioneer home with a thatched roof, built in 1951: the first purpose-built structure in Canada to commemorate Ukrainian settlement.

name: Tawayik Lake
summary: A lake south of Astotin ringed by aspen and meadow, with a 15.1-kilometre loop trail and views of grazing elk and plains bison.

name: Wood Bison Trail
summary: A difficult 15.6-kilometre loop through aspen forest south of Highway 16 — the only trail in the park where you can see wood bison.

name: Oster Lake
summary: A waterfowl sanctuary with a five-site backcountry campground on its west shore, a 4-kilometre walk on the Shirley Lake Trail.

name: Wahkotowin Visitor Information Centre
summary: The park's visitor centre off Highway 16, opened in 2019, with exhibits made with Indigenous communities, including a bison-hide Star Blanket.

name: Long Beach
summary: The unit's best-known stretch of sand, for surfing and beach walks. Dogs are allowed on a leash north of the Green Point Rocks only.

name: Rainforest Trails A and B
summary: Two one-kilometre loops of boardwalk and stairs through old temperate rainforest on either side of Highway 4, with interpretive panels.

name: Shorepine Bog Trail
summary: An 800-metre boardwalk loop with no stairs, floating on a bog where shore pines grow stunted and twisted.

name: Florencia Bay
summary: A sandy bay reached by the 2.5-kilometre Nuu-chah-nulth Trail from Kwisitis, with panels on Nuu-chah-nulth teachings along the way.

name: Radar Hill
summary: The site of a Second World War radar station, with the memorial to the Korean War battle of Kapyong and the highest viewpoint in the Long Beach Unit.

name: Broken Group Islands
summary: A maze of islands, sheltered channels and shell beaches in Barkley Sound, reached only by boat. Camping from May to September on six designated islands.

name: Benson Island
summary: A Broken Group island for walking, with a self-guided tour of archaeology that dates people's use of the island back more than 5,000 years.

name: Pachena Bay
summary: The northern trailhead of the West Coast Trail, near Bamfield, where hikers attend the pre-hike briefing before setting out.

name: Kwisitis Visitor Centre
summary: 'The other end of the beach': exhibits on land, sea and people, a longhouse replica and a deck over Wickaninnish Beach for whales, storms and surfers. Reduced hours in winter.

name: Sidney Spit
summary: A sand spit on Sidney Island, a 20-minute summer foot-ferry ride from Sidney: beaches, a lagoon that is an Important Bird Area, a campground and the park's only overnight dock.

name: East Point
summary: Saturna Island's eastern tip, a Whale Trail site for watching orcas, seals and Steller sea lions from shore. A community museum fills the old fog alarm building.

name: Mount Warburton Pike
summary: A summit with wide views over the Gulf Islands, at the top of a long, winding road on Saturna Island.

name: Winter Cove
summary: A Saturna Island day-use area. The 1.5-kilometre Xwiwxwyus Trail loops through forest and salt marsh to a viewpoint over Boat Pass.

name: Narvaez Bay
summary: One of the least disturbed bays in the islands, ringed by regenerating Douglas fir and Garry oak–arbutus woodland, with a walk-in or paddle-in campground.

name: Mount Norman
summary: A 2.4-kilometre trail on the Penders, from Ainslie Point Road or Canal Road, climbing 244 metres to a viewpoint over the islands.

name: Princess Margaret (Portland Island)
summary: A boat-access island with three backcountry campgrounds linked by a 7-kilometre perimeter trail. Shell middens around its shore recall a former First Nations village.

name: Russell Island
summary: The 1.2-kilometre Haumea Trail passes Coast Salish clam gardens and the Mahoi house, one of the last Hawaiian homesteads in the region.

name: D'Arcy Island
summary: Coves, cobble beaches and arbutus forest on a former colony for Chinese immigrants with leprosy. Seven first-come campsites, reached by water only.

name: SG̱ang Gwaay Llnagaay (Nan Sdins)
summary: The village on Anthony Island, a World Heritage Site: standing and fallen poles, house pits and longhouse posts and beams. Check in at the Watchmen cabin first.

name: G̱andll K'in Gwaay.yaay (Hotspring Island)
summary: Hot water seeps from at least 26 vents at 32 to 77 °C; three pools were rebuilt after the 2012 earthquake drained the old ones. No camping or pets.

name: Hlk'yah G̱awG̱a (Windy Bay)
summary: On Lyell Island: the 2013 Legacy Pole, a longhouse built during the 1985 blockade, and a trail to Sitka spruce estimated at 800 to 900 years old.

name: K'iid Xyangs Ḵ'iidaay (Burnaby Narrows)
summary: A narrow passage known for the marine life seen from a kayak drifting through. Its Haida name was restored in 2022. No camping along the narrows.

name: T'aanuu Llnagaay (Tanu)
summary: Village site where house depressions and fallen, moss-covered posts trace the layout of 25 to 40 longhouses. Outside the reserve but within the Haida Heritage Site, under the same rules.

name: Haida Heritage Centre, Skidegate
summary: The heritage centre at Ḵay Llnagaay on Graham Island, where the Gwaii Haanas office is based.

name: Mount Logan
summary: Canada's highest mountain at 5,959 metres, in the Icefield Ranges. It can be seen only from the park's remote interior, on flightseeing tours or expeditions.

name: Kaskawulsh Glacier
summary: A great valley glacier flowing from the icefields. Its retreat in 2016 sent its meltwater to the Alsek instead of the Ä’äy Chù, a rare case of river capture.

name: Observation Mountain
summary: Beyond the end of the 22.5-kilometre Ä’äy Chù West trail, a long, demanding route-finding climb leads to its top and views over the Kaskawulsh Glacier.

name: Thechàl Dhâl' (Sheep Mountain)
summary: The mountain above the Ä’äy Chù valley where Dall's sheep winter and are often seen from the visitor centre in spring and autumn. Its face is closed to all access.

name: Kathleen Lake (Mät’àtäna Män)
summary: A clear lake below the Kluane Range, with a day-use shelter, the accessible Kokanee Trail and a boat launch. The steep King's Throne trail climbs to a cirque above.

name: St. Elias Lake
summary: An easy 7.6-kilometre return walk through forest to a subalpine lake, with a primitive campsite of four tent pads; a popular overnight trip.

name: Nàłùdäy (Lowell Glacier)
summary: A surging glacier whose past advances dammed the Alsek River and flooded the valley; Lowell Lake lies at its toe.

name: Soldier's Summit
summary: A 1-kilometre trail to the site where the Alaska Highway was officially opened in 1942, a kilometre north of the Thechàl Dhâl' Visitor Centre.

name: Kluane National Park and Reserve Visitor Centre
summary: In the Da Kų Cultural Centre in Haines Junction: exhibits, trip planning and backcountry registration. Open from May to September.

name: Thechàl Dhâl' Visitor Centre
summary: In the Ä’äy Chù valley, an hour north of Haines Junction on the Alaska Highway, with exhibits made with local First Nations and spotting scopes for sheep.

name: Pine Lake
summary: An aquamarine sinkhole lake 60 km south of Fort Smith, with a sandy beach, the park's campground, rental cabins, canoe launch and the Dark Sky Circle.

name: Salt River Day Use Area
summary: Picnic ground 24 km south of Fort Smith above the Salt River, with the Dëldël Kué shelter, trailheads and red-sided garter snakes emerging in late April and May.

name: Salt River Meadows lookout
summary: A bench and lookout on the 2.2-kilometre loop through wildflower meadows beside a saline stream, starting across the road from the Salt River day-use area.

name: Lane Lake
summary: A lake south of Pine Lake at the end of the 6.5-kilometre Lane Lake Trail. The trail was closed in 2026 after the 2023 fires; check first.

name: Sweetgrass Landing
summary: On the Peace River, the start of the 14-kilometre walk to Sweetgrass Station, a 1950s–70s bison management station with corrals and heritage buildings in the delta meadows.

name: Lake Claire
summary: One of the major lakes of the Peace-Athabasca Delta, which rises when floods on the Peace and Athabasca rivers back water into the delta.

name: World's largest beaver dam
summary: A dam about 775 metres long across its face, visible from space, holding back run-off from the Birch Mountains. No road or trail: days of trekking or a chartered sightseeing tour.

name: Wood Buffalo National Park Visitor Centre, Fort Smith
summary: Exhibits, trip planning, backcountry and fishing permits, canoe and paddleboard rentals and a gift shop. Open seasonally from May; brochures in the lobby when closed.

name: 70 Mile Butte and Eagle Butte
summary: A short, steep loop climbs to wide views over the Frenchman River valley; the gentler Eagle Butte loop is known for wildflowers and birds of prey.

name: Top Dogtown
summary: A 750-metre hard-surfaced loop at Ecotour pull-off 2 across a black-tailed prairie dog colony. The park and its surroundings are the only place in Canada the species lives wild.

name: Timbergulch
summary: A 15-kilometre loop from Ecotour pull-off 3 through three glacier-cut coulee bottoms where the park's bison often linger. Five to six hours, difficult.

name: Two Trees Day Use Area
summary: Start of the Two Trees loop, a 4-kilometre introduction to the prairie, and the Riverwalk along the Frenchman River's cliffs and riverbank plants.

name: Larson Trail
summary: A 1.5-kilometre mowed loop at Ecotour pull-off 6 past traces of early ranching, with views of the Frenchman River.

name: Frenchman Valley Coulee Centre
summary: Beside the West Block campground: shade, a place to cook and eat, and the base for park programs. Open as a day-use shelter in winter.

name: Badlands Parkway
summary: An 11-kilometre single-lane paved road along an escarpment in the East Block, with six viewpoints over the Rock Creek badlands. Open to vehicles 1 May to 31 October.

name: Valley of 1000 Devils
summary: A 10-kilometre return trail from Rock Creek across Hellfire Creek into the badlands, where it can be up to 10 degrees hotter than the surrounding prairie.

name: Grasslands National Park Visitor Centre
summary: In Val Marie, near the West Block: maps, road and weather conditions, entry passes, campground check-in and backcountry registration.

name: Waskesiu Lake and Main Beach
summary: The lake and the beach at the centre of Waskesiu, the only community inside the park, with heritage buildings from the 1930s nearby.

name: Grey Owl's Cabin, Ajawaan Lake
summary: The 1930s cabin of Archibald Belaney (Grey Owl) and Anahareo, with their graves nearby. Reached on the 20-kilometre Grey Owl Trail or by paddling across Kingsmere Lake.

name: Kingsmere Lake
summary: A large, clear lake north of Waskesiu ringed by seven backcountry campgrounds; wide open water means crossings can be unsafe in wind.

name: The Narrows
summary: Where a current keeps Waskesiu Lake thin-iced all winter, giving the first open water of spring and a gathering place for waterfowl in late April and early May.

name: Height of Land Tower
summary: A 15-metre lookout tower beside Highway 263 over the mixed-wood forest around Shady Lake and Bear Trap Creek.

name: Spruce River Highlands
summary: An 8.5-kilometre loop across aspen-covered hilltops to a lookout tower above the Spruce River.

name: Boundary Bog Trail
summary: A 2-kilometre loop through knob-and-kettle country and spruce and tamarack into the heart of a boreal bog.

name: Amyot Lake and the Sturgeon River valley
summary: Aspen parkland and sedge meadows on the park's west side, often visited by the free-ranging Sturgeon River plains bison herd.

name: Prince Albert National Park Visitor Centre
summary: On Lakeview Drive in Waskesiu: backcountry registration, fishing permits, trout tags and entry passes. Open all year, with reduced winter days.

name: Waskesiu Nature Centre
summary: A 1935 heritage building in the Waskesiu townsite. Closed in winter; it reopens on the May long weekend.

name: Clear Lake and Wasagaming Main Beach
summary: The spring-fed lake and the beach and pier of Wasagaming, the park's townsite, with restaurants, rentals and lakeshore paths.

name: Ominnik Marsh
summary: A 0.5-kilometre loop on a floating boardwalk through a marsh of bulrushes and beavers, on the edge of Wasagaming.

name: Lake Audy Bison Enclosure
summary: A 500-hectare fenced prairie holding about 40 plains bison, viewed by car from the road through it. Visitors must stay in their vehicles.

name: Grey Owl's Cabin
summary: The cabin at Beaver Lodge Lake where Archibald Belaney (Grey Owl) lived for six months in 1931. A 14.8-kilometre return hike or bike ride.

name: Bald Hill
summary: Reputed to give one of the best views in the park, from the eastern escarpment over the farmland below. A difficult 11-kilometre return trip.

name: Lake Katherine
summary: A lake and picnic site east of Wasagaming, with a 3.5-kilometre loop trail.

name: Whirlpool Lake
summary: A lake and small primitive campground on Highway 19, 15 kilometres from Wasagaming.

name: Moon Lake
summary: A 9.5-kilometre loop through big spruce and fir along the lakeshore, with a primitive campground about 30 minutes from Dauphin.

name: Kippan's Mill
summary: A 1.3-kilometre loop to the site of the last sawmill in the park, in the high country off the Parkway.

name: Beach Ridges
summary: A 3.5-kilometre loop over oak- and hazel-covered ridges that were the shores of glacial Lake Agassiz.

name: Riding Mountain National Park Visitor Centre
summary: In Wasagaming, on Treaty 2 land: exhibits and visitor services. In the off season it opens Friday to Monday only.

name: Cape Churchill
summary: The northern tip of the park on Hudson Bay, where polar bears gather in autumn waiting for the ice. Seen from tundra vehicles and aircraft; the tip itself is strictly protected.

name: Thompson Point
summary: A point on the park's Hudson Bay shore south of Cape Churchill, beside the tidal flats that shorebirds and waterfowl use on migration.

name: Broad River compound
summary: One of two bear-proof fenced compounds Parks Canada owns in the park, with basic water and washroom facilities. Reached by canoe, aircraft or helicopter.

name: Owl River compound
summary: Parks Canada's southern fenced compound near the Hudson Bay shore, used for research, park work and safe camping by arrangement with the park.

name: Nester One research camp
summary: A privately owned fenced research camp south of Cape Churchill, which Parks Canada lists as an emergency shelter.

name: Parks Canada Visitor Centre, Churchill
summary: In Churchill's heritage railway station: exhibits on Wapusk and the region's history, a life-size polar bear maternity den, and talks. Seasonal hours.

name: The Grotto
summary: A sea cave cut by waves into the dolomite cliff, with underwater entrances from Georgian Bay. About an hour's round walk from the Cyprus Lake parking lot.

name: Indian Head Cove
summary: A rocky cove of clear water beside the Grotto, favoured by swimmers and scuba divers, with sea caves and the Natural Arch to the west.

name: Halfway Rock Point
summary: A point on the Georgian Bay Trail looking north to Flowerpot Island and Bear's Rump Island in Fathom Five National Marine Park.

name: Cyprus Lake
summary: The inland lake at the heart of the park's campground, circled by an easy 5-kilometre trail past stumps from early-1900s fires. Motorboats are banned.

name: Halfway Log Dump
summary: A rugged white cobble beach under sheer cliffs, a kilometre's walk from the end of the gravel Emmett Lake Road. Parking reserved in summer.

name: Singing Sands
summary: A Lake Huron day-use area on Dorcas Bay with fragile dunes, a fen boardwalk among orchids and insect-eating plants, and the Wild Garden Trail to an alvar.

name: Stormhaven
summary: One of the park's two backcountry camping areas, nine tent platforms on the Bruce Trail above Georgian Bay, reached on foot from Cyprus Lake.

name: Little Dunks Bay Lookout
summary: A viewing platform over a secluded cove of Georgian Bay, 800 metres along the Bruce Trail from the Visitor Centre through cedar forest.

name: Parks Canada Visitor Centre, Tobermory
summary: Shared with Fathom Five: exhibits, a film, a 20-metre lookout tower and short trails. A five-minute walk from Tobermory harbour.

name: Fairy Lake
summary: An inland lake on northern Beausoleil, circled by the 2.5-kilometre Fairy Trail, the park's must-hike loop, with a self-guided audio tour in the Parks Canada app.

name: Chimney Bay
summary: A sheltered bay at the north end, popular with anchored boats, with a backcountry campground and access to the rugged northern trails.

name: Honeymoon Bay
summary: A small sand beach with a marked swimming area at the north tip of Beausoleil, with backcountry campsites and sunsets over Georgian Bay.

name: Long Bay
summary: The view at the end of the mossy Dossyonshing Trail, one of the island's more challenging walks.

name: Little Dog Channel
summary: A narrow channel off northern Beausoleil, followed by the Cambrian Trail through pine forest as an extension of the Fairy Trail.

name: Tonch Point
summary: A peninsula on the east side of the island, reached from Cedar Spring by the narrow 3.8-kilometre Treasure Trail, with three backcountry campgrounds.

name: Lookout Trail
summary: A 1.5-kilometre trail in the south of the island with views over Georgian Bay and a platform looking into the forest canopy.

name: Christian Beach
summary: A beach on Beausoleil Island with four remote cabins for two, a composting toilet and ice delivered daily.

name: The Tip
summary: The southernmost point of mainland Canada: a shifting sand spit reached by a 1-kilometre loop from the shuttle stop. Swimming and wading here are banned because of strong currents.

name: Tip Tower
summary: An observation tower at the Tip exhibit area, reopened in 2025 after its guard rails were restored, looking over the forest, the beaches and Lake Erie.

name: Marsh Boardwalk
summary: A 1-kilometre floating loop through cattails, ponds and lily pads, with an observation tower and telescopes. Turtles, muskrats, frogs and dragonflies; canoes and kayaks for hire nearby.

name: DeLaurier Homestead and Trail
summary: A 1.2-kilometre loop past the DeLaurier homestead, telling 10,000 years of human history on the point, from the First Peoples to homesteaders, farmers, fishers and cottagers.

name: Tilden Woods Trail
summary: A 1-kilometre loop on boardwalks through mature swamp forest and savannah, with spring wildflowers such as spring beauty and mayapple.

name: Woodland Nature Trail
summary: A 2.75-kilometre loop through the park's oldest forest, with a side path to the redbud trees that flower near the end of May.

name: Northwest Beach
summary: A beach on the west shore with a pavilion that can be rented for the day. Closed from 1 November to 31 March.

name: Middle Island
summary: An 18.5-hectare island in Lake Erie, the southernmost land in Canada, added to the park in 2000. Strictly protected; no landings from 1 March to 1 September and no tours.

name: Point Pelee Visitor Centre
summary: Exhibits, a theatre, the Nature Nook bookstore and park staff; the free shuttle to the Tip leaves from here. Seasonal: closed from 2 November 2026 to 31 March 2027.

name: Hattie Cove (Bii to bii gong)
summary: A sheltered inlet, 'water between two rocks' in Anishinaabemowin, that stays calm on Superior's roughest days. The campground, visitor centre and canoe rentals are here.

name: Horseshoe Bay
summary: A crescent of golden sand and driftwood between granite headlands, reached by the accessible 1.2-kilometre Boardwalk Beach Trail past the dunes.

name: Southern Headland Trail
summary: A rugged 2.2-kilometre return walk onto bare rock jutting into Lake Superior, with views of Hattie Cove, Pulpwood Harbour and Horseshoe Bay and tiny arctic-alpine plants.

name: Manito Miikana
summary: 'The Spirit Trail': a 2-kilometre climb through a rocky ravine to two viewing decks over Lake Superior and the Pic River dunes.

name: Halfway Lake
summary: An inland lake circled by Bimose Kinoomagewnan, the 'Walk of Teachings', where elders' stories and youth artwork tell the Seven Grandfather Teachings.

name: Pulpwood Harbour
summary: A harbour of islands and inlets just outside Hattie Cove, a paddle for calm days only.

name: White River Suspension Bridge
summary: A bridge 23 metres above Chigamiwinigum Falls on the Coastal Hiking Trail: an 18-kilometre, full-day return hike from Hattie Cove.

name: Oiseau Bay
summary: A bay on the Coastal Hiking Trail, with campsites and a colony of the endangered Pitcher's thistle.

name: Hattie Cove Visitor Centre
summary: The hub for park programmes, the park store and backcountry information; open daily in summer.

name: Mallorytown Landing
summary: The park's mainland base on the Thousand Islands Parkway: visitor centre, boat launch, oTENTiks, picnic grounds, a lookout with the Thanksgiving Address carving and 2 kilometres of trails.

name: Jones Creek
summary: A network of mainland trails, from a 20-minute walk to a 2-hour hike, through tall pines, rock faces and lookouts. Open all year.

name: Landons Bay
summary: Six trails through fields, forest and wetland; the view from its Lookout Trail has long been called the best natural view in the Thousand Islands.

name: Grenadier Island
summary: Reached most easily from Mallorytown Landing, with trails at Central, North and East leading to historic buildings and the old township road. Possibly the Toniata of French accounts.

name: Gordon Island
summary: One of the Navy Islands, with oTENTiks and docking for campers; the nearest launch for paddlers is Misty Isles Lodge.

name: McDonald Island
summary: One of the Admiralty Islands near Gananoque, with oTENTiks and campsites, and one of the few islands where generators are allowed.

name: Thwartway Island
summary: An island in the Admiralty group, reached by paddlers from the Gananoque Municipal Marina.

name: Georgina Island
summary: An island beneath the Thousand Islands International Bridge, where the river narrows into strong currents and heavy boat traffic.

name: Cedar Island
summary: One of the park's Kingston islands, crowned by Cathcart Tower, a round stone Martello tower.

name: Vista Trail
summary: A 1.5-kilometre trail to a two-level viewing platform over the Little Rouge Creek and Rouge River valleys, one of the best places to see Toronto's autumn colours.

name: Mast Trail
summary: A 2.5-kilometre route over a wooded ridge on a 200-year-old logging road, with rare Carolinian forest; it links Glen Rouge with Twyn Rivers Drive.

name: Glen Eagles Vista
summary: A short trail to views of the Rouge River and Little Rouge Creek and a provincially significant bluff of sediments 13,000 to 30,000 years old. Parking closed November to May.

name: Cedar Trail and Beare Wetlands
summary: A 4.5-kilometre loop from restored wetlands with snapping turtles and waterbirds up into cedar forest above Little Rouge Creek. Access from Zoo Road was closed in 2026.

name: Rouge Marsh and Rouge Beach
summary: Toronto's largest remaining marsh and a sand beach at the river mouth on Lake Ontario, with a pedestrian bridge. Closed for construction since November 2025.

name: Woodland Trail
summary: A 3.5-kilometre walk along the Rouge River through forest and meadow, known for beavers, past traces of a cottage area flooded by Hurricane Hazel in 1954.

name: Bob Hunter Memorial Park
summary: Trailhead for the Monarch Trail through rare cedar savannah and the Tallgrass Trek past restored wetlands and meadows, named for the environmental campaigner Bob Hunter.

name: Harvest Trail
summary: A 5.1-kilometre family trail through crop fields, marsh and woodlots in the park's farmland, between the 19th Avenue and Black Walnut day-use areas.

name: Le Passage Lookout
summary: The park's best-known view, along Wapizagonke Lake from the Parkway. Closed for reconstruction; reopening is scheduled for spring 2027.

name: Vide-Bouteille Lookout
summary: An easily reached Parkway lookout over Wapizagonke Lake, with a giant red chair.

name: Les Cascades
summary: A stream with many natural pools, reached by trail near the Shewenegan picnic area: a favourite spot to eat on the rocks and cool off.

name: Waber Falls (Chutes Waber)
summary: A 27-metre waterfall reached by paddling 4.6 kilometres up Wapizagonke Lake, then hiking 3.4 kilometres; about three hours each way.

name: Lac du Caribou
summary: One of four large lakes in the western backcountry that hold only brook trout, with canoe-camping sites and scuba diving by free permit.

name: Lac Édouard
summary: A lake with a beach, picnic area and boat rental, about 12 kilometres from the Rivière à la Pêche campground; site of Quebec's first experimental forest.

name: Lac aux Chevaux Lookout
summary: Red chairs above both arms of Lac aux Chevaux, reached all year on the Lac Solitaire or Lac aux Chevaux trails from Rivière à la Pêche.

name: W8banaki and Andrew lodges
summary: Heritage buildings of the Laurentian Club on Lac à la Pêche; the W8banaki, built between 1886 and 1914, is the oldest in the park. A 3.7-kilometre trail from Saint-Gérard.

name: Rivière à la Pêche Service Centre
summary: Beside the Rivière à la Pêche campground, 6 kilometres from the Saint-Jean-des-Piles entrance, in the sector open all year; firewood is sold here in winter.

name: Cap Gaspé
summary: Land's End: a concrete lighthouse of 1950 on a 95-metre cliff, at the end of the Les Graves trail or a 4-kilometre walk or ride from L'Anse-aux-Amérindiens.

name: Grande-Grave heritage site
summary: The last buildings of a Gaspé cod-fishing village: the Hyman & Sons general store and the Dolbel-Roberts house, open with guide-interpreters in summer.

name: Anse-Blanchette
summary: The Blanchette house and its fishing outbuildings in a small cove, reached on the Les Parages loop from Grande-Grave.

name: Mont Saint-Alban
summary: An observation tower at 285 metres, looking out over sea and cliffs, reached by loops from Petit-Gaspé beach or, more steeply, from Cap-Bon-Ami.

name: Cap-Bon-Ami
summary: A pebble beach beneath the cliffs, good for seabirds and for the view of Cap Gaspé.

name: Penouille
summary: A sand spit in Gaspé Bay with a beach warm enough for swimming, a rare low-lying taiga on La Taïga trail and a visitor centre at its entrance.

name: Fort Peninsula
summary: The only completely preserved Second World War shore battery open to the public in Quebec, with guns, tunnels and storerooms of the Gaspé naval base.

name: La Chute
summary: A short, steep loop through maple and cedar groves to a 17-metre waterfall, from a car park on Route 132 between the North and South areas.

name: Le Castor
summary: A level stone-dust trail beside beaver ponds, with an observation platform, on a former stretch of Route 132 that is being returned to nature.

name: Penouille Visitor Centre
summary: At the entrance to the Penouille sand spit on the Gaspé Bay side, with park information, a Parks Canada shop and a sheltered picnic area.

name: Île aux Perroquets
summary: A lighthouse station of 1888 among puffins and razorbills. A Parks Canada guide tells the keepers' story; the keeper's house is now an inn.

name: Île Nue de Mingan
summary: A bare island of limestone monoliths, with a 9-kilometre shoreline walk and the remains of Basque ovens. Number of hikers limited; book with the boat operator.

name: Anse des Érosions, Île Quarry
summary: The archipelago's best-known flowerpot rocks, reached by a path through barrens and bogs.

name: Anse des Bonnes Femmes, Île Niapiskau
summary: Monoliths nicknamed the crocodile, the owl and the wedding cake, the tall Madame de Niapisca, and fossils about 465 million years old.

name: La Grande Île
summary: The largest island in the archipelago, with two clusters of monoliths and a 27-kilometre shoreline loop of about twelve hours.

name: Île du Fantôme
summary: A short trail through Arctic and alpine plants that are rare this far south, reached past the cliffs of Île du Havre.

name: Île du Havre
summary: Cliffs, a 17-kilometre shoreline loop and Ôasis units. Once the site of a fur-trading post; the Anse des Noyés campground is closed until further notice.

name: Petite île au Marteau
summary: The lighthouse station of 1915, with rare northern plants, a stop on the guided excursion to the Betchouane islands.

name: Havre-Saint-Pierre Reception and Interpretation Centre
summary: At 1010 promenade des Anciens: trip planning, tide information and the only place besides Longue-Pointe to pick up a camping permit.

name: Longue-Pointe-de-Mingan Reception and Interpretation Centre
summary: At 625 rue du Centre: information and camping permits for the western islands, whose boats leave from Longue-Pointe.

name: Dickson Falls
summary: The park's most popular trail: a 1.5-kilometre loop of boardwalk and stairs down a fern-filled ravine to its most photographed waterfall.

name: Third Vault Falls
summary: The park's highest waterfall, 16 metres, at the end of a 3.7-kilometre trail downhill through mixed forest. Allow three to four hours return.

name: Laverty Falls
summary: A curtain waterfall with a swimming hole below, 2.5 kilometres along a moderate trail.

name: Alma Beach
summary: Next to Alma village and the Headquarters area: at low tide the flats run out more than a kilometre to the water's edge.

name: Point Wolfe Covered Bridge
summary: The only covered bridge in a Canadian national park, at the site of the old sawmill village. Closed for repairs from 8 September to December 2026.

name: Herring Cove
summary: A beach reached by stairs, one of the places Parks Canada recommends for watching the tide come in and go out.

name: Matthews Head
summary: A 4.5-kilometre loop to a headland with wide coastal views and a sea stack.

name: Caribou Plain
summary: A 2.1-kilometre loop past beaver ponds to a raised bog with carnivorous plants.

name: Headquarters Visitor Centre
summary: In a 1950 heritage building above the east entrance near Alma: trip planning, campsite bookings and a gift shop. Open all year.

name: Wolfe Lake Visitor Centre
summary: At the west entrance, where the connector road from the Fundy Trail Parkway joins Route 114. Open from mid-May to mid-October.

name: Kellys Beach
summary: A 1.2-kilometre boardwalk across salt marsh and lagoon to a barrier beach on the Northumberland Strait. Lifeguards and a canteen in summer; no pets.

name: Callanders Beach
summary: A shallow lagoon behind a barrier beach, good for wading, paddling and clam digging, with a giant wigwam for Mi'gmaq programmes and the Mi'gmaq Cedar trail. Dogs allowed on a leash.

name: The Bog
summary: A 1.8-kilometre trail onto a raised peat bog, through forest and past fresh water.

name: Pointe-à-Maxime
summary: A paddle-in backcountry site on the Kouchibouguacis River, 2.5 kilometres from Cap-Saint-Louis wharf, and a base for visiting the seals in the Blacklands gully.

name: Sipu
summary: A backcountry site on the Kouchibouguac River, its Mi'gmaq name meaning river: about 5.5 kilometres by canoe from Ryans or 5 kilometres on foot from Pijeboogwek.

name: Petit-Large
summary: A primitive campground in a forest clearing, open all year; in winter a ski-toboggan helps haul gear the 3.5 kilometres from Pijeboogwek.

name: South Kouchibouguac
summary: The park's main campground, with serviced sites and oTENTiks, 5 kilometres from Callanders Beach.

name: Visitor Reception Centre
summary: At 186 Route 117 near the park entrance: information, exhibits including the Ventura memorial, and a gift shop. Pijeboogwek nearby serves winter visitors.

name: Skyline Trail
summary: From the top of French Mountain a level path crosses the plateau to a boardwalk on a headland cliff high above the Gulf: 6.5 km out and back or an 8.2 km loop. Watch for moose and whales.

name: Fishing Cove
summary: A 6 km descent from 355 metres to a grassy cove and cobble beach, once a Scottish fishing settlement and now the park's only wilderness campsite.

name: Lone Shieling
summary: A replica Scottish crofter's hut at the start of a short loop through 350-year-old sugar maples in the Grande Anse Valley, one of the park's most protected areas.

name: Beulach Ban Falls
summary: A 21-metre cascade 50 metres from the Aspy trailhead, at the end of a side road off the Cabot Trail. The Aspy trail follows the Aspy fault from here.

name: Mary Ann Falls
summary: A cascade popular for swimming, reached by a trail along an old alignment of the Cabot Trail on the eastern side of the park.

name: Franey
summary: A climb from near sea level to 423 metres, where a lookout faces the Clyburn Brook canyon and the Atlantic coast from Cape Smokey to Ingonish. A 4.5 km lower loop or 13 km full loop.

name: Middle Head
summary: A 5.3 km trail out to headland cliffs at Ingonish, overlooking the Atlantic, Cape Smokey and Ingonish Island.

name: Chéticamp Visitor Centre
summary: The western entrance: exhibits on the park, passes and programme tickets, and Le Nique nature bookshop. The Acadian Trail climbs 365 metres from across the road. Mid-May to late October.

name: Ingonish Visitor Centre
summary: The eastern entrance, opened in 2014, beside Freshwater Lake. Passes, programme tickets and park information. Mid-May to late October.

name: Kejimkujik Lake
summary: A lake dotted with islands, once called Fairy Lake. Canoes and kayaks can be hired in the park, and one backcountry site lies on Ritchie Island.

name: Merrymakedge Beach
summary: A sandy beach on Kejimkujik Lake with an encampment site, a café and, in fall, winter and spring, a fine view of the southern night sky.

name: Big Dam Lake
summary: Old-growth hemlocks more than 300 years old grow along the north side of the lake. The Big Dam parking lot is the start of the Liberty Lake backcountry trail.

name: Peter Point
summary: A secluded sandy point reached by a 1.9 km trail through maple and hemlock. The petroglyph site here may be entered only with authorisation.

name: Jeremys Bay
summary: The main campground's bay on Kejimkujik Lake, with serviced and unserviced sites, oTENTiks and the Slapfoot Trail along the shore.

name: Visitor Centre and Mill Falls
summary: Passes, permits, backcountry check-in and Mi'kmaw birchbark canoes. Behind it, a 2 km return trail follows the Mersey River to Mill Falls. Open late May to 31 October.

name: Harbour Rocks
summary: At Kejimkujik Seaside, the end of a 2.8 km trail through coastal forest and barrens to rocky islets where harbour and grey seals haul out; a viewing scope is provided.

name: St. Catherines River Beach
summary: A beach of white quartzite sand that squeaks underfoot, seen from a platform on the Harbour Rocks Trail. Closed during the piping plover nesting season.

name: Kejimkujik Seaside trailhead
summary: The parking area, washrooms and start of the Harbour Rocks and Port Joli Head trails, on St. Catherines River Road near Port Joli.

name: Main Station
summary: The island's operational hub, centred on the weather station, where every visitor arrives. Restrooms and drinking water; many of the island's best-known places are within walking distance.

name: West Light ponds
summary: Freshwater ponds near West Light on the island's western half, where the freshwater lens surfaces and horses come to drink. Parks Canada suggests them for quiet reflection.

name: South Beach
summary: The long ocean-facing beach. Hard-packed sand makes it the easiest walking on the island; fixed-wing planes land on the beach runway.

name: North Beach
summary: The northern shore opposite Main Station, where grey seals haul out and where boats anchor offshore before a wet landing by zodiac.

name: Bald Dune
summary: A bare dune beside Iris Pond towards the east end of the island, reached from North Beach.

name: Lake Wallace
summary: Once a 22-kilometre saltwater lagoon; blown sand filled it until it ceased to be a permanent lake in 2011. The area still floods after heavy rain or storm overwash.

name: East Light and the East Spit
summary: The lighthouse near the eastern end of the island, beyond which the flat East Spit runs out towards the submerged East Bar.

name: West Spit
summary: The flat sand tip at the western end, where vegetation and dunes have been spreading in recent years.

name: Cavendish Beach and Dunelands
summary: The park's best-known beach, supervised in summer, with a 2.4 km trail past dunes and freshwater ponds and a floating boardwalk.

name: Oceanview Lookoff
summary: A lookout over red sandstone cliffs at the start of the Gulf Shore Way West to North Rustico. The cliff edges beyond the fences are closed.

name: Green Gables Heritage Place
summary: The farm that inspired Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of Green Gables, part of L.M. Montgomery's Cavendish National Historic Site, with the Haunted Wood and Balsam Hollow trails. Separate admission.

name: Robinsons Island
summary: Reached by a 3.2 km gravel trail along the causeway from Brackley Beach, with a 5 km loop of lookouts, beach access and mountain-bike features.

name: Covehead Harbour Lighthouse
summary: A small lighthouse above a sandy dune path by Covehead Harbour, on the Gulf Shore Parkway at Stanhope.

name: Dalvay-by-the-Sea
summary: A Victorian summer house built between 1896 and 1899, now a national historic site and inn, at the east end of the Gulf Shore Parkway.

name: Greenwich Dunes Trail
summary: A 4.6 km walk across old homestead fields and a floating boardwalk over Bowley Pond to the island's largest sand dunes, with interpretive signs.

name: Greenwich Beach
summary: A long white-sand beach on the Greenwich peninsula, supervised in summer, with a solar-powered beach facility and the Greenwich Interpretation Centre nearby.

name: Western Brook Pond
summary: A landlocked fjord between cliffs rising to 670 metres above sea level, with waterfalls spilling from the plateau. A 3-kilometre trail leads to the dock for a two-hour boat tour.

name: The Tablelands
summary: A barren orange mountain of the Earth's mantle. An easy 4-kilometre return trail runs along its base to Winter House Brook Canyon; Parks Canada leads two-hour guided walks.

name: Gros Morne Mountain
summary: The park's highest point, 806 metres. A difficult 17-kilometre loop with 1,000 metres of climb crosses its arctic-alpine summit; closed 1 May to 27 June.

name: Green Point
summary: Seaside cliffs of tilted sea-floor layers that mark the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary. Off Route 430, 500 metres north of the campground; best at low tide.

name: Lobster Cove Head Lighthouse
summary: A century-old lighthouse above Bonne Bay with an exhibit on lightkeepers and local history, short headland trails, tide pools and a favourite spot for sunsets.

name: Broom Point Fishing Premises
summary: The restored summer fishing station where three Mudge brothers and their families fished from 1941 to 1975. Grounds open year-round; buildings when staff are present.

name: Trout River Pond
summary: A pond below the Tablelands, with a trail along its shore into their heart. One of only two ponds in the park where small motorboats are allowed.

name: Green Gardens
summary: A 4.5-kilometre trail across the Tablelands and down to a volcanic coastline, with a small primitive campsite on the cliff top.

name: Gros Morne Visitor Centre
summary: Near Rocky Harbour, open all year with reduced off-season hours: passes, permits, backcountry registration and trip advice.

name: Discovery Centre, Woody Point
summary: The park's geology exhibition and a Mi'kmaw exhibition from Miawpukek, with passes and permits. Open mid-May to mid-October; the Lookout Trail starts here.

name: Ochre Hill
summary: A former fire-watch hill near the middle of the park with a panoramic view; a nearby trail climbs to a look-off over Bread Cove and Clode Sound.

name: Sandy Pond
summary: A day-use area with a swimming beach, picnic tables and an easy 3-kilometre loop through boreal forest. Rated the darkest sky in the park, and a start for paddling trips.

name: Newman Sound
summary: The long, sheltered sound at the heart of the park, with the main campground, the Coastal Trail along its inner shore and a migratory bird sanctuary on its mud flats.

name: Mount Stamford
summary: A summit lookout reached by a 1.2-kilometre side trail about 9 kilometres along the Outport Trail, the park's longest, which runs 35 kilometres return from Newman Sound.

name: Minchins Cove
summary: The remains of a sawmilling settlement on the Outport Trail, reached on foot or by boat, with backcountry campsites and a dock.

name: Malady Head
summary: A steep 3.4-kilometre trail from Malady Head Campground to a cliff-top view over Southwest Arm, the Eastport causeway and Alexander Bay.

name: Louil Hill
summary: A 3.7-kilometre loop for walkers and cyclists through forest damaged by insects and browsing, with stairs up to a bare granite top above Alexander Bay.

name: Dunphy's Pond
summary: The park's largest pond, off the Trans-Canada Highway, reached by a 10-kilometre return trail or by canoe; backcountry sites on its shore and island.

name: Terra Nova Visitor Centre
summary: On the shore of Newman Sound: exhibits, a marine touch tank, programmes, boat tours and kayak trips with a local operator, and the start of the Coastal Trail. Open mid-May to mid-October.

name: Saglek Fiord
summary: The park's southern boundary and the usual way in. Gneiss around Saglek Bay is among the oldest dated rock on Earth, 3.9 billion years old.

name: Silluak (North Arm)
summary: A branch of Saglek Fiord between fjord walls about 900 metres high. Day trips from Base Camp land here to walk past old caches and hunting blinds to waterfalls and a sandy-beached lake.

name: PitukKik (Nakvak Brook)
summary: A traditional Inuit route from the Labrador coast to Ungava Bay, marked at its mouth by a commemorative inuksuk. The full trek runs about 68 kilometres over five or six days.

name: Nachvak Fiord
summary: A deep fjord in the heart of the range, its cliffs rising more than 900 metres straight from the water, with the site of an old Hudson's Bay Company post.

name: Mount Caubvick
summary: The highest peak in mainland Canada east of the Rockies, 1,652 metres, on the Quebec border, where it is called Mont D'Iberville. Small glaciers cling to the cirques around it.

name: Ramah Bay
summary: The remains of a Moravian mission where Inuit and Europeans lived side by side from 1871 to 1908, near the ancient kitjigattalik–Ramah chert quarries.

name: Mealy Mountains (Akami-Uapishkᵁ)
summary: Glacially rounded summits of bare rock rising to 1,180 metres above Lake Melville, with mountain tundra at the heart of the park reserve.

name: The Wunderstrands
summary: Some 50 kilometres of remote sandy beach where the park meets the Labrador Sea, around Cape Porcupine. Reached by kayak or boat from Cartwright or Rigolet.

name: English River
summary: One of the park's three named wild rivers, with Atlantic salmon and brook trout.

name: North River
summary: A wild river through the park's boreal forest, with Atlantic salmon and brook trout.

name: White Bear River
summary: A wild river of the park reserve, home to Atlantic salmon and brook trout.

name: Firth River
summary: About 130 navigable kilometres from Margaret Lake to the Beaufort Sea, through a succession of canyons with Class IV rapids. Rafted over one or two weeks.

name: Imnairvik (Sheep Creek Base Camp)
summary: Parks Canada's camp beside the Firth at Sheep Creek: prospector tents inside an electric bear fence, an Inuvialuit cultural host, and day hikes to tors such as Wolf Tors and Halfway to Heaven.

name: Engigstciak
summary: A hill rising from the coastal plain near the Firth, used by hunters to scan the land for thousands of years and the oldest known site in the park.

name: British Mountains
summary: Never glaciated, they fill about two-thirds of the park, with ridges and peaks from 860 to 1,680 metres that grow more rugged towards the west.

name: Nunaluk Spit
summary: Where Firth River trips end, on the Beaufort Sea. The one place in the park where wood fires are allowed, in Parks Canada's fire pits or a fire pan, with driftwood only.

name: Komakuk Beach
summary: An air access point on the coast, and the site of the first northern DEW Line station, built by the American army in the 1950s.

name: Stokes Point (Iqpiqyuuq)
summary: A coastal air access point for hikers, with the eroded remains of Inuvialuit camps and houses and the site of a later DEW Line station.

name: Clarence Lagoon (Qaininqvik)
summary: A lagoon near the Alaska border where a trading post stood at the turn of the twentieth century; the remains of camps, graves and houses survive on its shore.

name: Van Tat (Old Crow Flats)
summary: A Ramsar wetland of more than two thousand shallow lakes, used by up to half a million waterfowl a year. Its northern edge forms the southern third of the park.

name: Old Crow River
summary: The park's southern boundary in part, and a canoe route in early summer or autumn. Eroding banks along it are internationally significant ice-age fossil sites.

name: Ts'ī̀vī Shùh (Timber Hill)
summary: A hill rising among the lakes of the Flats inside the park; its Gwich'in name is the official one.

name: Mount Clement
summary: One of the peaks of the British Mountains in the park's north, where tundra covers the high ground and caribou cross on their spring and autumn migrations.

name: Ammerman Mountain
summary: A summit at the park's western edge, beside the border with Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.

name: John Tizya Centre
summary: In Old Crow, south of the park: exhibits on the park, the Porcupine caribou and Beringia, elders' recorded stories, and the Parks Canada office where you register.

name: Thomsen River
summary: One of the most northerly navigable rivers in North America: 160 kilometres of Class 1 water through the park's lushest valley, with no rapids. Paddled from late June to late July.

name: Head Hill
summary: A network of kill sites on a hill above the meeting of the Thomsen and Muskox rivers, with more than 500 muskox skulls, 29 food caches and 17 tent rings.

name: Muskox River
summary: The Thomsen's main tributary, flowing in from the west through poorly drained wetlands and frost polygons; a common place to end a river trip.

name: Mercy Bay and McClure's Cache
summary: Where HMS Investigator was trapped from 1851 to 1853. The cache and three crew members' graves are on the shore inside the park; the wreck lies in the bay, just outside.

name: Castel Bay
summary: A deep inlet of M'Clure Strait on the north coast, where many river trips end. One of the places polar bears are most likely to be met.

name: Shoran Lake
summary: Site of the oldest archaeological finds in the park: Pre-Dorset tent rings from about 1500 BC, with scrapers, harpoon heads, needles and muskox bones.

name: Nangmagvik Lake
summary: One of the larger lakes in the park, holding landlocked arctic char.

name: Náįlįcho (Virginia Falls)
summary: The South Nahanni plunges more than 90 metres around a central rock stack. Day flights land here; interpreters lead a walk to a viewpoint above the Sluicebox Rapids.

name: Cirque of the Unclimbables
summary: Granite walls and spires in the Ragged Range, among them the Lotus Flower Tower. Reached by floatplane to Glacier Lake and a strenuous six-kilometre, unmaintained route to Fairy Meadows.

name: Glacier Lake
summary: One of only two day-use landing sites, below the Ragged Range, with food caches for climbers bound for the Cirque.

name: Gahnįhthah (Rabbitkettle Hotsprings tufa mounds)
summary: Canada's largest tufa mounds, terraces built by 20 °C spring water. A special preservation area, seen only on hikes led by park staff.

name: Gahnįhthah Mįe (Rabbitkettle Lake)
summary: A staffed summer landing site and the start of many river trips, two to three days' paddling above Náįlįcho. Up to four species of loon and red-necked grebes can be seen here.

name: The Gate and Pulpit Rock
summary: In Third Canyon the river turns a hairpin through a narrow gap beside a 460-metre limestone wall, with the pinnacle of Pulpit Rock on the east side.

name: Deadmen Valley
summary: A calm stretch between Second and First canyons below the Tlogotsho Plateau. Its mineral licks draw Dall's sheep; stopping at the licks is prohibited.

name: First Canyon
summary: The last and highest of the four canyons, cut through resistant limestone, with the park's highest vertical walls.

name: Kraus Hotsprings
summary: Two sulphurous springs at the foot of First Canyon, named after Mary and Gus Kraus, who lived here from 1940 to 1971. Camping closes from 1 August.

name: Nahanni Parks Canada Office, Fort Simpson
summary: The park's main office in Łįįdłįį Kų́e (Fort Simpson): reservations, registration and fee payment. Open daily in July and August.

name: Nááts'įhch'oh Tué (Moose Ponds)
summary: Turquoise ponds below the sacred mountain, start of the 21-day, 600-kilometre South Nahanni descent, which opens with 50 kilometres of Class II–IV rapids, the Rock Gardens.

name: Mount Nááts'įhch'oh (Mount Wilson)
summary: The pointed peak that gives the park its name, a place of spiritual power for the Shúhtaot'ine. A special preservation zone, closed to entry; seen from the Moose Ponds.

name: Ǫtaa Tué Fehto (Divide Lake)
summary: Start of the Broken Skull River: about 150 kilometres of mostly Class I–II whitewater to Rabbitkettle Lake, six to ten days. A former outfitter's cabin stands by the lake.

name: Nı́onep'eneɂ Tué (Backbone Lake)
summary: A turquoise lake used as a base for off-trail hiking. Formerly Grizzly Bear Lake: Elders caution against speaking the bear's name. Dı́ga Dezene Deé (Black Wolf Creek) starts nearby.

name: Túoch'ee Tué (O'Grady Lake)
summary: Start of the Natla River trip: floatplanes land at a sandy peninsula on the south shore, inside the park. A Shúhtaot'ine harvesting place for fish and moose.

name: Pı̨́ı̨́p'enéh łéetǫ́ǫ́ Tué (Broken Skull Lake)
summary: One of seven lakes long used as floatplane access points, in the Broken Skull country in the south of the park.

name: Tuededéveh Tué (Clearwater Lake)
summary: A lake below the large mountain Parks Canada lists as Tuededéveh Shúh (Clearwater Mountain), used as an access point.

name: Dechįbaa Tué (Margaret Lake)
summary: A lake access point near the Broken Heart Plateau and Three Sisters Mountain.

name: Hornaday River
summary: The park's largest river, 360 kilometres from the upland tundra to Amundsen Gulf. Paddled in 8 to 12 days in July, starting at Hornaday Lake or on the main river.

name: Uyarsivik (Cache) Lake
summary: Where most Hornaday paddling trips end, above the canyons. A floatplane landing lake, with a cabin and a set of Parks Canada's red chairs.

name: La Roncière Falls
summary: A 21-metre waterfall in the last of the Hornaday's three canyon sections. The canyons below Uyarsivik Lake, falls included, are currently closed to visitors.

name: Seven Islands Lake
summary: One of the lakes in the north-west of the park where floatplanes can land.

name: Kaché Kaɂá (Pike's Portage)
summary: The historic overland route from the East Arm to the barrens, unmarked and unmaintained, travelled by Indigenous Peoples for generations to meet the caribou.

name: Ɂedacho Tué (Artillery Lake)
summary: "The lake of the big caribou crossing", where the tree line meets the barrenlands, with many cultural sites; some, such as Timber Bay's village site, are restricted or closed.

name: Crystal Island
summary: An island in Artillery Lake, one of the stopovers offered on flightseeing tours to the edge of the barrens.

name: Hak'ós Tué Tsën Tłazį (Charlton Bay)
summary: A bay of the East Arm of Great Slave Lake, one of the paddling destinations Parks Canada lists.

name: Nıtłër Nu Naá Tłazį (Wildbread Bay)
summary: A bay on the East Arm, linked to McLeod Bay by the Lost Channel Portage, a traditional route; a paddling destination.

name: Siltaza Lake
summary: Where most paddlers on Tędhul Dezé, the Snowdrift River, take out. Below Austin Lake the river has Class IV and V rapids and a waterfall, for expert paddlers only.

name: Eileen Lake
summary: A lake on the park's southern boundary and one of the paddling destinations Parks Canada lists away from Great Slave Lake.

name: Akshayuk Pass
summary: The 97-kilometre corridor between Pangnirtung Fiord and North Pangnirtung Fiord along the Weasel and Owl rivers. Unmarked, with nine emergency shelters about a day apart.

name: Qaiqsualuk (Thor Peak)
summary: A peak above the Weasel River whose sheer face is the best-known landmark in the pass. Climbing it is for self-reliant, experienced parties only.

name: Qattaujannguaq (Mount Asgard)
summary: Twin barrel-shaped rock towers above the pass north of Summit Lake, which Parks Canada counts among the most distinctive peaks of the Canadian Shield.

name: Tasiruluk (Summit Lake)
summary: The high point of Akshayuk Pass, feeding the Weasel River south and the Owl River north. Overlord to Summit Lake and back is the most common five- to six-day hike.

name: Crater Lake
summary: A lake near the southern end of the pass. Parks Canada's guided spring day trips from Pangnirtung stop below it before walking on to cross the Arctic Circle.

name: Windy Lake
summary: Site of a staff cabin and emergency shelter. The suspension bridge here was washed out by flooding in 2008, so hikers keep to one side of the river.

name: Overlord Peak
summary: The peak at the southern end of the pass, above Pangnirtung Fiord, where outfitters from Pangnirtung bring walkers in. Overlord is the southernmost of the nine shelters.

name: Penny Ice Cap
summary: About 6,000 square kilometres of ice and snow at the centre of the park, feeding the glaciers, rivers and lakes around it.

name: Piqalujaqtuuq (Greenshield Lake)
summary: The largest lake in the park, set in vegetated tundra in the west and important wildlife habitat. Few visitors travel this far from the pass.

name: Panniqtuuruluk (North Pangnirtung Fiord)
summary: The northern gateway to the pass, reached by boat or snowmobile from Qikiqtarjuaq. Parks Canada advises travelling three to four hours inland before camping.

name: Helena Island
summary: One of the Berkeley Group off northern Bathurst Island, crowned by a large cairn built in 1853 by a British naval expedition searching for Franklin.

name: Berkeley Group
summary: The islands off Bathurst Island's north coast, all within the park, where Franklin search parties left cairns and supply depots between 1850 and 1854.

name: Stokes Range
summary: The hills of northern Bathurst Island, part of the Arctic Cordillera and the island's highest ground.

name: Erskine Inlet
summary: On the inlet's shore stands Dome Camp, two hard-sided domes with one shelter open to the public as a base camp, emergency supplies and an aircraft landing site.

name: Dundee Bight
summary: Site of a Parks Canada camp of two cabins, one of them open to visitors and for emergencies, used for monitoring and community use.

name: Île Vanier
summary: One of the Governor General Islands west of Bathurst Island, taken into the park together with Massey Island, Alexander Island, Île Pauline and Île Marc.

name: Tanquary Fiord
summary: The park's main operations station and visitor hub, with an airstrip, visitor centre, kitchen tent, Weatherhaven accommodation and a small museum of 1960s research finds.

name: Gull Glacier
summary: A glacier visible from the Tanquary Fiord camp, one of many that fill the views on hikes from the station.

name: Kettle Lake
summary: An area of ancient cultural sites near Tanquary Fiord, with a Parks Canada walking-tour guide.

name: Ad Astra Ice Cap
summary: With the Viking Ice Cap, the centre of the park's best-known hike, a nine- to ten-day loop from Tanquary Fiord.

name: Lake Hazen (Tasialuk)
summary: One of the largest and deepest lakes north of the Arctic Circle, in a warmer polar oasis rich in plants, wildlife and archaeological sites. A staffed Parks Canada camp stands on its shore.

name: Henrietta Nesmith Glacier
summary: One of the glaciers that feed Lake Hazen, above the Henrietta River delta on the lake's north-western shore.

name: Barbeau Peak
summary: The highest mountain in Nunavut and the Canadian Arctic. A goal for strong, self-sufficient ski-touring parties in spring.

name: Fort Conger
summary: Remains of the base camps of Nares, Greely and Peary on Lady Franklin Bay, 1875–1909. A special preservation area: visits only with Parks Canada staff.

name: Ward Hunt Island
summary: A small island off the north coast, with a Parks Canada camp, emergency radio and airstrip; a base for research and a departure point for North Pole expeditions.

name: Cape Columbia
summary: Northern tip of Ellesmere Island and the most northerly land in Canada, used as a starting point for attempts on the North Pole.

name: Bylot Island
summary: The park's largest island, across Eclipse Sound from Pond Inlet: mountains, icefields and 16 glaciers, a Migratory Bird Sanctuary since 1965.

name: Sermilik Glacier
summary: A glacier on Bylot Island's south coast, the destination for short boat or snowmobile trips from Pond Inlet for visitors with only a day or two.

name: Aktineq Glacier
summary: A Bylot Island glacier crossed on skis in Parks Canada's film on mountain travel in the park. Late March to early June is the season for ski touring.

name: Kangiqluruluk (Oliver Sound)
summary: A great fiord south of Pond Inlet with steep cliffs and valley glaciers near the water, ice-free relatively early; good for boating, kayaking, camping and day hikes.

name: Nalluata imanga (Navy Board Inlet)
summary: The main sea route to the Borden Peninsula and Cape Hay; glaciers drop abruptly to the shore north of Low Point.

name: Cape Hay
summary: Seabird cliffs on Bylot Island's north-west coast. Thick-billed murres and kittiwakes nest here; in summer the colony may be viewed only from a boat.

name: Mala River
summary: A Borden Peninsula valley beside a route from Arctic Bay to Pond Inlet proposed for guided snowmobile trips. From 1 June to 31 August, non-motorised travel only.

name: Elwin Inlet
summary: An inlet on the Borden Peninsula's north coast near the Baillarge Bay seabird cliffs. The coast south-west of it closes to visitors from 16 June to 31 July for floe-edge harvesting.

name: Wager Bay
summary: A tidal fjord more than 150 kilometres long, with eight-metre tides. Outfitters' boats offer the safest way to see polar bears, seals, belugas and, occasionally, walrus, orcas, bowheads and narwhals.

name: Reversing Falls
summary: Reversing tidal falls at the head of Wager Bay, where the bay meets Ford Lake; one of the features Parks Canada points visitors to, with old habitation sites nearby.

name: Ford Lake and the Hudson's Bay Company post
summary: The trading post opened in 1925, the first run by an Inuk manager. Its old buildings stand; visit only with an approved guide or Parks Canada staff.

name: Douglas Harbour
summary: A harbour on Wager Bay with a Government of Nunavut wildlife research cabin, also used by Inuit harvesters; protected cultural sites lie on its north shore.

name: Nuvukliit and the Savage Islands
summary: An island archipelago in Wager Bay, among them Main Savage Island, with a mission site and other protected cultural sites.

name: Piksimanik River
summary: A river flowing into Wager Bay, followed by the North and South Piksimanik over-snow routes into the park; protected cultural sites lie along its lower reaches.
